summary: Specifies how to encode characters outside US-ASCII, and indicate language, in HTTP header field parameters. It is compatible with a simplified profile of the RFC 2231 encoding used in MIME. It replaces RFC 5987.

eli5.summary: Web headers can only use basic letters. This is a trick for writing other alphabets, such as accented letters, in them.

questions: how to encode non-ascii characters in http headers
what is the title* parameter in http
what does utf-8 in a header parameter mean
subtitle: How an HTTP header parameter can carry non-ASCII text and say which language it is in.

tldr.problem: HTTP header field values cannot easily carry characters outside US-ASCII, and HTTP says nothing about which character encoding a field value uses.
tldr.mechanism: A parameter name ending in an asterisk can hold an ext-value: a character encoding name, an optional language tag and a percent-encoded value, separated by single quotes. Producers MUST use UTF-8.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5987 and moves it to Historic. The RFC reports use in four header fields, including Content-Disposition.

today: RFC 8187 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 5987, which it moves to Historic, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Header Parameters Need Help
sections.content:
Using characters outside the US-ASCII character set in HTTP header fields is non-trivial. HTTP discourages such characters in field values and puts them into the obs-text ABNF production. It also stays silent about a default character encoding, so any use would need to be specific to the field definition or rely on out-of-band information.

Some APIs make this worse by assuming an encoding. The RFC notes that the XMLHttpRequest API uses the type ByteString, which in effect means ISO-8859-1.

RFC 2231 already defined an encoding for parameters in MIME header fields. This document specifies an encoding for HTTP that is compatible with a simplified profile of it, and it can be applied to any HTTP header field that uses the common name=value parameter syntax. It does not apply to message payloads such as multipart/form-data.
sections.eli5: Header lines were built for plain English letters. If you want to write a name with an accent, you need a secret code that everybody agrees on.

sections.title: What Was Kept from RFC 2231
sections.content:
The RFC goes through RFC 2231's MIME extensions and says which apply to HTTP.

  • Parameter continuations are dropped. They deal with length limits on MIME headers, and those limits do not apply to HTTP.
  • Character encoding and language information are kept, as a simple subset.
  • Language in encoded words is dropped. The HTTP/1.1 specification of the time had deprecated the RFC 2047 encoded-word forms.

Two further changes tighten RFC 2231. Recipients MUST support UTF-8, because RFC 2231 had no mandatory-to-implement encoding and senders could not tell which to use. And the character encoding can no longer be left out.
sections.eli5: Imagine a big rulebook for school mail. This one keeps only the pages that help with funny letters and throws away the rest.

sections.title: The Extended Value Syntax
sections.content:
Extended parameter values are usually flagged by a parameter name that ends in an asterisk, such as title*. That is only a convention: the header field's own definition has to opt in explicitly.

The value, called ext-value, has three parts separated by single quote characters: the REQUIRED character encoding name (charset), the OPTIONAL language tag, and the actual value (value-chars). Encoding names and language tags are US-ASCII and matched case-insensitively.

Characters that are not in attr-char are first turned into octets with the stated encoding, and those octets are then percent-encoded. attr-char is a token that excludes the asterisk, the single quote and the percent sign. Producers MUST use UTF-8; other encodings are reserved for future use. The quoted-string notation is not allowed, for backwards compatibility with RFC 2231.

Recipients should handle encoding errors, such as malformed percent escapes or undecodable octets, robustly. The RFC does not mandate a behavior. Ignoring the parameter, stripping the bad octets, or substituting a replacement character such as U+FFFD are all acceptable.
sections.eli5: The special label says three things: which code book was used, which language it is, and then the scrambled word itself. Anything unusual gets written as a percent sign and two letters or digits.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The plain forms are title=Economy and title="US-$ rates". For the pound sign U+00A3, UTF-8 gives the octets C2 A3, which become %C2%A3. The space is not in attr-char, so it becomes %20. The result is title*=utf-8'en'%C2%A3%20rates.

A second example adds the euro sign U+20AC, whose octets are E2 82 AC, and leaves the language empty: title*=UTF-8''%c2%a3%20and%20%e2%82%ac%20rates. HEXDIG allows upper and lower case, so recipients must understand both. The language is optional but the character encoding is not.
sections.eli5: A pound sign gets written as %C2%A3, a bit like spelling out a hard word letter by letter so nobody gets it wrong.

sections.title: Guidance for Header Authors
sections.content:
A header field specification that uses this extension should say so, ideally by referencing this RFC and including the ext-value production in the ABNF for the parameter. Names ending in an asterisk should not be used for anything else, since some implementations already switch to this notation automatically for such names.

The extension ought to be used whenever the value is text and its language is known, because RFC 2277 requires that human-readable protocol text can carry language information. It ought also to be used whenever the value needs characters outside US-ASCII. A new parameter restricted to a subset of Unicode would be unacceptable.

On errors, each header definition must say whether parameters with the same name may repeat. The RFC suggests that the extended form takes precedence, so a sender can include both an ASCII title for legacy recipients and a title* for those that understand this specification.
sections.eli5: If you invent a new header, write down that it uses this trick. Send a plain version too, so old programs can still read something.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Carrying non-ASCII characters enables character spoofing, where a displayed value looks like something other than what it is. There are also known attacks related to decoding UTF-8. The RFC points to Section 10 of RFC 3629 for both topics.

Because one parameter can carry several language variants, a spoofing attack is also possible where the different language versions are not equivalent. Whether that works as an attack depends on the parameter. The RFC asks for no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Some letters from different alphabets look the same, so a trickster could make a word look like another one. Be careful what you trust on screen.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 5987
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 5987. The main changes are:

  • The title and introduction were rewritten.
  • The requirement to support ISO-8859-1 was removed. Internet Explorer 9 did not support it, and UTF-8 is enough to express all code points. Recipients are still encouraged to support it for legacy code.
  • The document no longer tries to define a generic parameter ABNF, because HTTP has no truly generic definition (whitespace handling differs).
  • An outdated note about error-handling defects was removed.

The implementation report lists four header fields using the encoding: Authentication-Control, Authorization (HTTP Digest), Content-Disposition and Link.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the rulebook. The authors dropped an old rule that nobody needed and tidied up the explanations.
